scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

The scenario involves a custody arrangement where the father has every other weekend and a weekday. In the specific incident, the mother called last Wednesday and asked the son to stay with her because a cousin was there. The father agreed but wanted to get the son back on Thursday. Now, the father is not getting the son on his scheduled weekend because the mother is taking him to a 4th of July party, and the father is expected to give up more time tomorrow.

The key points here are the custody agreement, the mother's frequent changes to the schedule, and the father's frustration. The father feels he's being taken advantage of because he's always accommodating. The mother's actions, like changing plans last minute and not allowing the father to adjust the schedule, seem to be causing conflict. 

The father's decision to keep the son during the visitation might be a reaction to the mother's previous behavior. However, custody agreements are legal documents, and deviating from them without agreement could be problematic. But in this case, the mother also didn't follow the original plan by taking the son to the lake instead of letting the father pick him up. 

The father's main concern is to have his scheduled time with the son. The mother's refusal to switch weekends and the 4th of July party might be seen as not respecting the agreement. The father's action could be a way to enforce the custody terms. However, is it morally acceptable to keep the son against the mother's wishes? 

Morally, the father is trying to protect his time with his son, which is important for the child's well-being. The mother's actions might be seen as manipulative or not in the child's best interest. However, the father should ideally work through the issue rather than unilaterally changing the schedule. But given the history of the mother altering the schedule, the father's action might be justified as a response to her behavior. 

But is it morally acceptable? The father is within his rights to enforce the custody agreement, but taking the child against the mother's wishes could be seen as overstepping. However, if the mother is not adhering to the agreement either, there might be a mutual issue. The father's action could be a way to ensure he gets the time he's entitled to. 

In terms of morality, the father's intention is to maintain a stable schedule for the child, which is positive. The mother's refusal to adjust might be a problem. So, the father's action might be morally acceptable as a response to the mother's non-compliance. However, there could be better ways to handle it, like mediation. But in the context of the scenario, the answer might lean towards 1 (morally acceptable) because the father is standing up for his rights after the mother's previous actions.
